# Robustness: is this engine's answer a property of the evidence, or of the engine?

*Generated by `scripts/phase1/20_robustness.py`. Do not hand-edit — regenerate it.*

The report concedes in §13 that the decision rule in §1 was written alongside the candidate work rather than pre-registered before it. That concession invites the obvious question: **were the rules shaped until they emitted the candidate we had already picked?** A reader cannot settle that by reading the rules — a fitted rule and an honest rule look identical on the page. It is settled by perturbing the engine and watching what moves. That is what this file does, and it runs in `run.sh`, so a result we would rather not publish cannot quietly fail to be published.

Two of the five experiments are **assertions**: they fail the build. Three are **descriptive** — they report what moved, including when the answer is unflattering.


Baseline: **7 of 17** candidates eligible (STRONG or CONDITIONAL); named candidate `C-NA` = **CONDITIONAL**.


## R1 — Gate ablation (descriptive)

Each rule is switched off in turn. If the funnel's shape is really the product of one rule, this is where it shows: one row will account for most of the rejections and the rest will be ornament.

Two columns, because they mean different things. **Changed outcome** is a candidate that became eligible once the rule was removed — the rule was the only thing stopping it. **Caught by another rule instead** is a candidate that stayed rejected but was picked up further down the chain: the removed rule was real, and redundant. Reading only the first column makes an over-determined engine look like an inert one.


| rule removed | eligible | named candidate | changed outcome | caught by another rule instead |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ablate G1_oncology | 5 | CONDITIONAL | `C-DQ`, `C-RAPA`, `N-MITOTIC` | — |
| ablate G2_pediatric | 7 | CONDITIONAL | — | — |
| ablate G3_renal | 7 | CONDITIONAL | `C-AMPK` | — |
| ablate G4_growth | 6 | CONDITIONAL | `C-RAPA` | — |
| ablate directionality | 7 | CONDITIONAL | — | `N-ASA`, `N-ISO`, `N-MITOTIC` |
| ablate eligibility | 7 | CONDITIONAL | — | `C-NAD`, `C-RT`, `N-AICAR`, `N-FIS`, `N-NAVI`, `N-NUC` |

### R1b — How over-determined is each rejection?

Each rejected candidate is tested against every rule *independently*, rather than stopping at the first rule that fires. The question is how many separate rules would reject it on their own. A funnel fitted to produce a chosen answer is fragile in a specific way: each rejection traces back to the one rule that was tuned. Rejections reached independently by two or three unrelated rules are not the kind of thing rule-fitting produces, because tuning the oncology gate does not also arrange for the eligibility rule and the directionality prerequisite to agree.


**9 of 10** rejections are reached independently by two or more rules.

| `N-MITOTIC` | `directionality`, `G1_oncology`, `G2_pediatric` | 3 |

### R1c — The scenario gate, switched on

The base case carries no `scenario` block — the three scenarios are separate case files — so the scenario gate cannot be ablated out of the baseline, and a row reporting "no change" would mislead. The honest test runs the other way: switch each scenario on and watch the gate work. **S2** is the branch in which the missense allele is a function lesion rather than an abundance problem, and it should retire the named candidate along with every other restore-class candidate.


| scenario | `restore` validity | eligible | named candidate | changed outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | `valid` | 7 | CONDITIONAL | — |
| S2 | `invalid` | 5 | REJECT | `C-NA`, `C-PBA` |
| S3 | `conditional` | 7 | CONDITIONAL | — |

**One observation across R1, R1b and R1c.** Under every gate ablation and every constraint perturbation the named candidate stays at **CONDITIONAL** — no weakening of any safety rule promotes it. Under S2 it is **REJECT**. Those two facts together are the point: the tier is not a gate product. STRONG additionally requires rescue evidence in disease-relevant cells at `evidence_distance >= 3`, and this candidate has neither, so no amount of loosening the gates can upgrade the strength of an evidence claim — while a change in the *scientific* premise, which is what the scenario encodes, retires the candidate outright. A reader worried that the engine was built to protect its answer should note that the only perturbation that moves the named candidate is the one that attacks the biology.



## R2 — Patient-constraint perturbation (descriptive)

One fact about the child is changed at a time, everything else held. A gate that produces the same output for every child is not doing work; a gate that changes the answer is patient-specific in the way an N-of-1 submission claims to be.

## R3 — Name blinding (assertion)

Every candidate's identifier and drug name is replaced by an opaque token and the list is shuffled before the engine sees it. If any verdict changes, some code path is reading the name — the engine would be recognising its favourite rather than assessing it.


**PASS** — 17 candidates blinded, 0 verdict differences.


## R4 — Synthetic probes (assertion)

Six candidates with known-correct answers are injected alongside the real ones. The twin tests favouritism: a compound identical to the named candidate in every field that the engine reads, under a different name, must receive the identical verdict. The mirror and the poisoned probes test that each gate actually bites when it should — a gate that never rejects anything is not a gate.


| probe | what it is | expected | observed | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `PROBE-TWIN` | same properties as the named candidate under another name | see text | CONDITIONAL at `passed` | PASS |
| `PROBE-MIRROR` | named candidate's twin, acting in the opposite direction | see text | REJECT at `directionality` | PASS |
| `PROBE-ONC` | twin that also increases chromosomal instability | see text | REJECT at `G1_oncology` | PASS |
| `PROBE-PED` | twin with no approved or credible pediatric path | see text | REJECT at `G2_pediatric` | PASS |
| `PROBE-RENAL` | twin that is nephrotoxic | see text | REJECT at `G3_renal` | PASS |
| `PROBE-GROWTH` | twin that is anti-anabolic (G4 can only flag, never reject) | see text | CONDITIONAL at `passed` (flags: G4_growth) | PASS |

## R5 — Leave-one-source-out on the therapeutic chain (descriptive)

The chain this hypothesis depends on runs niacin → NAD+ → SIRT2 → BubR1 acetylation → residual BubR1. Each supporting paper is removed in turn. A PMID that leaves an edge with no source at all is a **single point of failure**: if that one paper does not survive scrutiny, the chain is cut at that link.


2 distinct path(s) from D1 to P: E14 → E15 → E16 → E17; E14 → E15 → E16b → E17


| paper removed | paths still fully sourced | edges left unsourced |
|---|---|---|
| PMID 19407811 | 2 / 2 | — |
| PMID 24825348 | 0 / 2 | `E15`, `E16` |
| PMID 25285631 | 2 / 2 | — |
| PMID 32386566 | 0 / 2 | `E14` |
| PMID 38009412 | 2 / 2 | — |

**2 single point(s) of failure.** Removing any one of these leaves no complete path from the intervention to the endpoint:

- **PMID 24825348** — North BJ 2014, *SIRT2 induces the checkpoint kinase BubR1 to increase lifespan*. Sole source for `E15`, `E16`.
- **PMID 32386566** — Pirinen E 2020, *Niacin Cures Systemic NAD+ Deficiency and Improves Muscle Performance in Adult-Onset Mitochondrial Myopathy*. Sole source for `E14`.

This is the most consequential result in this file and it is not a flattering one. The therapeutic chain is not a web of mutually reinforcing evidence; it is a series circuit. Two papers carry it, and one of them carries the entire SIRT2→BubR1 core. We report this rather than counting the chain's total citation list, which is larger and would give a misleading impression of redundancy. The practical consequence is stated in the report's limitations: a reader who doubts either paper should treat the hypothesis as unsupported rather than weakened, and the first two stages of the decisive experiment (§6) are designed to measure those two links directly in the patient's own cells rather than inherit them from the literature.

## What this does not show

Perturbing an engine tests the engine, not the biology. R1–R4 would look exactly like this if every property value fed into them were wrong: the gates would still bite, the twin would still match, the names would still not matter. What they establish is narrower and worth stating exactly — the verdicts follow from the recorded fields by a rule that treats an unnamed compound the same as the named one. Whether those fields are *true* is the job of the mechanism chain (§3), the citation check, and the claim ledger. R5 is the only experiment here that touches the evidence, and it tests dependency structure, not whether a given paper is right.

One further limit: the probes are built by mutating the named candidate, so they test the gates along the axes we thought to mutate. A gate failure on an axis we did not think of would not appear here.
